title: The Tide Clerk
subtitle: A Mystery of the Cornish Harbour, 1923
description: On the morning after the spring tide, Captain Silas Trewin is found dead at the foot of the lock steps. The coroner calls it a fall in the dark. But Evelyn Marsh, the harbour board's tide clerk, notices what the inquest ignores: the lock gate was opened twice in the night, and only once was logged. Every clue is a document or an object the reader sees alongside her—a stopped pocket-watch, a wet coat, a receipt, the tide tables themselves. The solution turns on the tide alone: the precise time at which a body dropped from the steps would have been carried where it was found. Evelyn works it out from her own ledgers while being quietly squeezed out of her post. A fair-play mystery where the sea itself is the final witness.

editorReview.text: The Tide Clerk offers a meticulously crafted historical procedural where the tidal rhythm becomes a detective in its own right. The sensory precision is undeniable; you can practically taste the tar on the nets, and the confrontation with Nora Keast—her needle stopping mid-stitch—delivers a masterclass in showing rather than telling. Yet, the narrative occasionally settles into competence over urgency.
